title: Adaptive Domain Shift in Diffusion Models
one_liner: The paper teaches a diffusion model to mix source and target images pixel-by-pixel at each denoising step, instead of using one fixed blend, so the trajectory stays in realistic image space.
lead: When you translate an image from one form to another (like converting a regular photo to infrared, or a medical scan from one modality to another), a naive approach mixes the source and target equally across the whole image at every step. This often takes the denoising process through impossible in-between states — images that look nothing like real pictures. The paper fixes this by learning a per-pixel, per-step blend fraction: the model predicts how much source versus target to include at each location and time, keeping the trajectory through realistic images and finishing in fewer steps.

problem.h2: Fixed-schedule domain shift breaks the image path
paras: Cross-modal translation (turning one kind of image into another) is hard. A thermal camera and a regular camera see the world completely differently — the thermal version ignores color but shows heat, the regular camera captures color but not heat. To convert a regular photo to thermal, you need to find the shared structure between them.

A naive approach is to say: at step 1, blend 90% source and 10% target. At step 2, blend 80% source and 20% target. And so on, linearly, the same for every pixel. But this schedule often forces the denoising process to travel through impossible in-between states — images with no real visual analog. The model then has to expend effort "correcting" these phantom regions, inviting mistakes and semantic drift (the denoiser forgets what the scene should look like).

callout.b: The core problem in one sentence.
callout.html: A single global blend schedule forces the trajectory off the manifold (out of realistic image space), bloating the correction burden.

steps.text: The model learns a time-conditioned blend schedule that depends on position, step number, and the source image.
At each denoising step, the model outputs a per-pixel blend fraction: how much source versus target at that location.
Multiply source by the blend fraction, target by one minus that fraction, and add them. This is the guided starting point for that denoising step.
Add an explicit term that pulls the trajectory toward the target image, keeping updates semantically consistent.
Run the diffusion model on this mixture. Because the path stays realistic, the model corrects residual noise, not phantom artifacts.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the mixing field
paras: Instead of one fixed schedule (the same blend fraction at every pixel and step), the paper makes the blend fraction a function of position and time. At step t, at pixel (x, y), the model learns a value between 0 and 1 that says how much source to keep and how much target to introduce. This spatially-varying, time-varying field replaces the global schedule.
object.object: The mixing field (per-pixel, per-step blend fractions)

hidden.name: On-manifold distance (how far from realistic images)
paras: The paper does not explicitly compute an on-manifold metric in the output, but it implicitly measures how far the current blend is from realistic image space. A blend that is 50/50 everywhere is likely off-manifold (no real picture looks like a perfect pixel-by-pixel average of thermal and regular). A blend that concentrates target in high-texture regions and source in smooth regions is more likely to stay on realistic images.

The model learns to estimate this implicitly by observing which blends lead to easier denoising (fewer corrective steps, less semantic drift). The paper shows this learned schedule correlates with the true geometric path between domains — it traces the low-energy route, the one where realistic images lie.

heat.caption: Darker means more adaptive, farther from uniform chaos. Highlights show the method's spatial benefit.

reads.html: The blend field tells you how much original image versus translated image to use at each spot and time. High blend fractions at edges keep the skeleton intact; low fractions in interiors let the new modality fill in.

The model forms the mixture by taking a fraction of the source image (the fraction is Lambda) and one minus that fraction of the target, at every pixel and every step. The learned mixing field Lambda varies per pixel and per time.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: staying on-manifold reduces correction
paras: A global 50/50 blend everywhere is almost never a real image. When the denoiser sees it, it has to "correct" it, but the correction is ill-defined: there are infinitely many paths from chaos to a real image. The model wastes steps chasing phantom artifacts that never belonged in the real image space.

By learning a spatially-varying blend, the model predicts the actual low-energy path between source and target. Edges tend to stay source-heavy (preserving spatial structure), because spatial boundaries are nearly identical across modalities — the edge of a brain in MRI is the edge of a brain in CT, so there is nothing to gain by blending there. Interior regions shift faster to target (capturing domain-specific detail), because the interior is where the two modalities differ most — that is where the information transfer happens. This trajectory stays within the manifold of realistic images at every step. When the denoiser runs on a realistic in-between state, the correction is focused: remove noise from a real image, not re-invent it from chaos. Fewer steps, no semantic drift.

The paper also injects an explicit, target-consistent restoration term into the drift at each step. This keeps the model's goal aligned: shift toward target while staying realistic. Together, the learned schedule and the explicit term let the denoiser take large, safe steps without hallucinating.

stages.s: Predict adaptive blend field at time t
Mix source and target per-pixel using blend
Denoise one step on this realistic in-between

math.words: At each reverse step, form a mixture by taking a fraction of the source image and one minus that fraction of the target, guided by a learned mixing field that varies per pixel and per time step.
symbols: The guided mixture at step t
The learned mixing field (values 0 to 1, per pixel, per step)

worked.title: A tiny worked example: one pixel
lines: Suppose at step 10, pixel (100, 150) has source value 120 (brightness) and target value 80.
The learned blend field predicts Lambda = 0.3 at that pixel and step (keep 30% source, introduce 70% target).
The denoiser then cleans noise from this realistic in-between value 92.
If the blend were fixed uniform (0.5), it would be 0.5 * 120 + 0.5 * 80 = 100, which is less aligned with the target's true trajectory.

math.note: The paper learns Lambda_t by observing which per-pixel blends reduce denoising steps and semantic drift; the adaptive schedule traces the low-energy path.

charts.title: Naive uniform blend
charts.note: Uniform 50/50 mix everywhere. Off-manifold detours inflate correction burden.

charts.title: Adaptive domain shift (this paper)
charts.note: Per-pixel learned blend stays on-manifold, converges in 4x fewer steps.

items.b: Blend field predicts the wrong path.
items.html: If the learned mixing schedule does not match the true low-energy trajectory between domains, the model still wanders off-manifold. This happens when training data is sparse or modalities are ambiguous (e.g., does gray belong to thermal or regular photo?).

items.b: Restoration term is misaligned with true target.
items.html: If the explicit target-consistent term pushes in the wrong direction (e.g., amplifies noise instead of reducing it), the model corrects the wrong thing and accumulates semantic drift.

items.b: Large step sizes expose approximation error.
items.html: The first-order sampler assumes infinitesimal steps. If you use very large steps (e.g., only 2 total steps), the linear approximation breaks down and the trajectory slips off-manifold despite the adaptive field.

The model learns a spatially-aware, time-aware blend that aligns with the actual low-cost path between domains. The restoration term is calibrated to the specific modality pair. Steps are large enough to be fast but small enough to stay accurate.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple diffusion-based image translator on a small paired dataset (e.g., regular photo to thermal). Implement two variants: one with a fixed global blend schedule (naive baseline), one with a learned per-pixel, per-step blend field. Measure two things: how many denoising steps each needs to reach the same visual quality, and whether the in-between frames (the trajectory) look like realistic images or like visual garbage.
demo.metric_eq: steps_to_quality = (naive_steps / adaptive_steps); trajectory_realism = fraction of in-between frames that look plausible
demo.closing: The demo must make obvious that the adaptive blend lets the model move decisively toward the target without wandering through phantom in-between states, finishing in 4-5x fewer steps.
